title: "Cameras After the Smartphone"
subtitle: "Worldwide digital camera shipments and the DSLR-to-mirrorless handoff, 2010–2025"

date: 2026-08-29

<p><span class="kicker">Data Story &nbsp;·&nbsp; CIPA &nbsp;·&nbsp; Camera & Imaging Products Association</span></p>

<div class="lead">
<p>In 2010, the world's camera makers shipped 121.5 million digital cameras — the high-water mark of a category the smartphone was about to gut. By 2023, annual shipments had fallen 94%, to 7.7 million. Then something unusual happened: shipments rose for two straight years, the first back-to-back increase in nearly two decades, driven almost entirely by two very different products — professional-grade mirrorless bodies, and a pocket-sized point-and-shoot revival led by Gen Z.</p>
</div>

## Finding a real time series

CIPA, the Japanese trade association whose members include Canon, Nikon, Sony, Fujifilm, Panasonic, and Olympus/OM Digital, has published monthly worldwide shipment data since the 1990s and is the industry-standard source everyone from Statista to DPReview ultimately cites. The association's own historical PDF archive isn't set up for scraping, so the series below is reconstructed from CIPA's published monthly and annual releases as reported by CIPA itself and cross-checked against PetaPixel, DPReview, Nikon Rumors, and Statista, rather than pulled from a single downloadable file.

2007 is where a clean, comparable annual series becomes possible: that's the first year CIPA's own releases split shipments into "built-in lens" (compact) and "interchangeable lens" (DSLR-and-later-mirrorless) totals, and it's also the year worldwide shipments first broke 100 million units. Before 2007, comparable digital-era data exists (roughly 5 million units shipped in 1995, the digital camera's standing start) but isn't broken out by camera type, so it's mentioned qualitatively rather than charted.

Splitting that "interchangeable lens" total into DSLR and mirrorless separately is a harder problem, because CIPA didn't report the two as distinct categories in its own headline releases until well into the format's life. Mirrorless launched in September 2008 (Panasonic's Lumix G1) and was a rounding error for years afterward, so 2007–2011 below shows essentially all interchangeable-lens shipments as DSLR. From 2012 the mirrorless share is interpolated against known product milestones — Sony's a7 brought full-frame mirrorless in 2013; Nikon and Canon didn't commit to full-frame mirrorless systems of their own until 2018 — anchored to three points CIPA itself has published: mirrorless overtook DSLR within the interchangeable-lens category for the first time in 2020 (51.5%), reached 68.7% by 2022, and 80.5% by 2023. 2024 and 2025 are CIPA's own reported figures. The interpolated stretch (2012–2019, and 2021) is flagged in the chart note below; treat it as the shape of the transition rather than exact annual counts.

## The format war: who won the shrinking pie

The total collapsed, but the mix inside it changed even more dramatically. In 2010, compact point-and-shoots — the cameras smartphones killed first — still accounted for 109 million of the 121.5 million units shipped, with DSLRs and the still-new mirrorless format (Panasonic's Lumix G1, the first mirrorless model, had shipped roughly two years earlier) making up the remaining 12.5 million between them. By 2025, the compact category had shrunk to 2.4 million units but mirrorless had grown into the dominant force in the industry at 6.3 million units, while DSLRs — which Canon and Nikon have largely stopped developing — had fallen to just 691,000, kept alive mainly by Pentax and a market for cheap used bodies.

## Two different recoveries, one chart

The 2024–2025 uptick isn't one story but two. At the top of the market, mirrorless bodies keep getting more expensive and more capable, and buyers — increasingly professionals and serious enthusiasts rather than casual shooters — keep paying for them; shipment value has grown faster than unit volume for several years running. At the bottom, a cohort too young to have owned a point-and-shoot the first time around has been driving demand for compact cameras like the Fujifilm X100 series and screen-free novelties like the Camp Snap, treating a dedicated camera as a deliberate alternative to a phone rather than a worse version of one. Both trends show up as growth in the same chart, but they're selling to different customers for different reasons — which is presumably why CIPA's own 2026 shipment forecasts still describe a wide range (6.3–7.4 million interchangeable-lens bodies) rather than a confident single number.

---

**Sources:** Camera & Imaging Products Association (CIPA), worldwide monthly and annual digital still camera shipment statistics, as reported by CIPA and independently cited by PetaPixel, DPReview, Digital Camera World, Fstoppers, and Statista. 2025 figures reflect CIPA's full-year release (February 2026); 2026 references are CIPA's preliminary/forecast data as of mid-2026. The 2010 compact/interchangeable-lens split is drawn from CIPA's own reported totals for that year.
